intro: Grants and low-cost loans can pay for things a budget can’t. This page lists real programs, what each pays for, who can apply, and when — read from each agency’s own page. Programs open, close, and change; always confirm at the link before applying.

items.name: Community Facilities Direct Loan & Grant
items.pays: Public buildings and equipment. Its list includes police stations, prisons, fire departments and fire trucks — and community gardens, food pantries, community kitchens, food banks, and greenhouses.
items.who: Counties, cities, nonprofits, and tribes, for places of 20,000 people or fewer.
items.size: Loans up to 40 years; grants of 15% to 75% of the cost, depending on the community’s size and income.

items.name: Adult Treatment Court Program
items.pays: Starting or improving a drug or treatment court.
items.size: Up to $950,000 to start one; up to $1,025,750 to improve one.
items.note: A first step on Grants.gov is due Oct 30, 2026.

items.name: Opioid, Stimulant, and Substance Use Program (COSSUP)
items.pays: Treatment and recovery, including treatment inside jails and at release.
items.who: Counties, cities, states, tribes; rural counties have their own category.
items.size: Up to $1,000,000 over three years for a rural local government.
items.note: The 2026 round closed in September. Watch for the 2027 round.

items.name: State Revolving Funds (drinking water and clean water)
items.pays: Low-interest loans for water and sewer projects; part of some loans is forgiven. Includes separate money for lead pipes and for “forever chemicals” (PFAS).
items.note: Each state keeps its own priority list and dates.

items.name: Water & Waste Disposal Loans & Grants
items.pays: Drinking water, sewer, solid waste, and storm drainage.
items.who: Rural areas and towns of 10,000 people or fewer.
items.size: Long-term, low-interest loans; grants when funds allow.

items.name: WIFIA water loans
items.who: Public systems; small communities (25,000 or fewer) get easier terms.
items.size: Small-community projects of $5 million or more; up to 80% of the cost.

items.name: BUILD grants
items.pays: Road, bridge, and other surface transportation projects, and planning.
items.size: Rural projects from $1 million to $25 million.
items.match: Rural projects can be paid up to 100% by the federal share
items.note: The 2026 round closed in February. Watch for the next notice.

items.name: Safe Streets and Roads for All
items.pays: Road-safety action plans and safety projects.
items.note: The 2026 round closed in May; the agency says about $1 billion remains for the next round.

items.name: Assistance to Firefighters Grants
items.pays: Equipment, protective gear, training, and vehicles — paid straight to fire departments, including volunteer departments.
items.size: Up to $1 million for departments serving 100,000 people or fewer.
items.note: The last window ran May 19 – June 22, 2026. Opens about once a year.

items.name: Mutual Self-Help Housing (Section 523)
items.pays: Pays a nonprofit to guide groups of families who build each other’s homes; the families do most of the labor.

items.name: Home loans and repair help (Sections 502 and 504)
items.pays: Low-interest home loans for low-income rural families; repair loans to $40,000 at 1%, and repair grants to $10,000 for very-low-income owners 62 and older.

how.text: Before applying for any federal grant, a county or city needs a free SAM.gov registration and a Unique Entity ID. Allow at least 10 business days — sometimes weeks.
how.label: Grants.gov — registration

how.text: Spending $1,000,000 or more of federal money in a year triggers a special “single audit.”
how.label: 2 CFR 200.501

how.text: Open federal notices are searchable in one place.
how.label: Grants.gov — search

limits: A grant is not free money: most need a local match, staff time to apply and report, and someone to run the project.
Dates and amounts were read on the date shown and will change. Confirm at the link.
A program being listed here doesn’t mean a given project qualifies — eligibility turns on details only the agency can settle.
Grants pay for a project once. They rarely pay for running something year after year.
